paragraphs: A road stud is a small aluminium housing with reflective lenses set into sloping faces, bonded to the road surface. The slope is what matters: it presents the lens to oncoming headlights at the right angle and lets a tyre ride over the stud without tearing it out. Modelled as a flat disc it loses both properties.
The mesh is light at 5,072 polygons and 2,546 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the lens recesses and the sloped faces.

At $9 it suits road and highway visualisation, traffic safety presentation, civil infrastructure renders, urban and motorway scenes, and games. Road studs appear in long repeating lines, so the low weight is what makes the asset usable. On sale since 2023.

A military belt is a wide webbing strap with a heavy metal buckle, and the interest sits in three places: the buckle mechanism, the stitched keeper at the tail and the row of grommets or the slotted holes that let equipment hang from it. Those are what separate it from a dress belt, and this build carries all three.
The mesh is light at 12,692 polygons and 6,342 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the buckle and the webbing edge weave.

At $9 it suits military and law enforcement visualisation, character set dressing for film, television and games, uniform and equipment presentation, and reenactment reference. On sale since 2023, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard figure.

A warning sign is a triangle on a post, and everything that matters is regulated: the corner radius, the border width, the symbol proportions and the height of the plate above the ground. Those specifications differ by country, which is precisely why a correct sign locates a scene and a wrong one quietly breaks it.
The mesh is light at 12,924 polygons and 6,528 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the plate face as its own surface so a different symbol can be applied without remodelling.

At $9 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits road and street visualisation, traffic and highway engineering presentation, driving simulators and games, architectural exteriors and film set dressing. On sale since 2024.

A complete anatomy library is a different proposition from a single figure. Skeletal, muscular, vascular, nervous, respiratory, digestive and organ systems each have to be modelled separately and then have to agree with one another spatially, because the value is in being able to show one system inside another rather than in any single model.
That coherence across systems is the hard part and the reason a collection is worth more than the sum of its pieces. Bought separately from different sources, the layers never quite fit.

Two more collections sit on this page at $1199 each. This set at $1299 is aimed at medical and health education, clinical and patient communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research presentation and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2023.

A full body anatomy build has to hold up at two very different scales: the whole figure in one frame, and a single region filling the screen. That is why this model carries an extraordinary texture load - 776 maps in total, with 3 at 8192x8192, 138 at 4096x4096, 413 at 2048x2048 and 222 at 1024x1024. Each structure gets its own material rather than sharing an atlas.

The mesh runs 672,769 polygons and 675,417 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is what a complete figure needs when muscle bellies, tendon insertions and vascular paths all have to read correctly.

At $579 it is priced as a reference asset and used as one: medical and health education, clinical communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research and pharmaceutical presentation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2020.

A fairytale castle is a different building from a real one. Real fortifications are squat and grim; the storybook version has slender towers, conical roofs, banners and a courtyard that could hold a ball rather than a garrison. This build commits to that version, with the courtyard modelled as a usable space and grass grooming across the grounds.

It is a heavy asset at 2,558,180 polygons and 2,565,713 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. That density goes into the stonework, the roof tiling and the tracery, which is what a hero shot of a castle is examined for.

At $399 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits fantasy film and television, games, animation and previsualisation, book and poster illustration, and theme park and exhibition design. On sale since 2025.

A cable ship is built around one machine: the cable engine and the enormous turntables below deck that hold thousands of kilometres of cable. Above deck that shows as a bow sheave, a linear cable engine amidships and a clear working deck aft. It also has dynamic positioning thrusters, because the ship has to hold station in a swell.

The mesh runs 1,687,885 polygons and 1,883,588 vertices in quads and tris, and it arrives rigged. The UVs overlap, which is a sound economy on a hull built from repeated plating and identical fittings.
At $349 it suits subsea and telecommunications visualisation, offshore energy presentation, maritime industry marketing, documentary work and games. On sale since 2024.

A carrier without aircraft is a runway. This build includes the air group, which is what turns the ship into a functioning warship in a render: aircraft spotted on deck, in the deck park and by the islands, arranged the way a real deck cycle would leave them.

It is among the heaviest assets in the catalogue at 3,498,038 polygons and 3,736,063 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. That density is what lets a camera drop to deck level and still find real geometry in the aircraft, the deck fittings and the twin islands rather than flat stand-ins.

At $329 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, museum and exhibition material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2025.

paragraphs: The PT6 is a reverse-flow turboprop: air enters at the rear, flows forward through the compressor and combustor, then drives turbines that turn a propeller shaft at the front. That layout is counterintuitive and impossible to explain without a cutaway, which is exactly what this sectioned build provides.

The mesh runs 726,009 polygons and 724,890 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 91 texture maps - 57 at 4096x4096 and 34 at 2048x2048. That count exists because a sectioned engine shows machined faces, blade rows and internal ducting that all need their own treatment.

Three other builds sit on this page, from $249 for an uncut engine to $299 for an alternative section. Aimed at aviation training and maintenance material, aerospace marketing, technical education, museum displays and games. On sale since 2016.

A refinery is a forest of columns, drums, heat exchangers and pipe racks, and its visual character comes almost entirely from age: streaked insulation cladding, rust running down from flanges, faded paint on tank shells and stained concrete plinths. A clean refinery looks like a rendering exercise; a weathered one looks like an industry.

It is a very large asset at 3,004,941 polygons and 3,146,207 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is essential economy on a plant built from thousands of repeated fittings, and it keeps a site this size workable.

At $299 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits oil and gas visualisation, energy sector marketing, infrastructure and environmental presentation, documentary and news work, film and television, and games. On sale since 2025.

The Arleigh Burke class is the backbone of the American surface fleet, and its shape is set by the four fixed radar panels on the deckhouse and the vertical launch cells fore and aft. Porter is a Flight II ship, and the model carries the mast array, the gun mount, the boat davits and the helicopter deck.

It runs 1,558,756 polygons and 1,724,629 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 26 texture maps all at 8192x8192. Twenty-six maps at the largest size is a serious commitment, and it is what carries hull staining and deck markings along a warship without visible repetition.

A rigged build sits on this page at $229. The static model at $289 covers naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, museum material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2017.

Firefighters almost never appear alone. A fire scene needs a crew: someone on a hose, someone at the pump panel, someone carrying equipment, all in full turnout gear with helmets, BA sets and boots. Building and rigging that crew one figure at a time is a long job, and rigging bulky protective clothing is harder than rigging ordinary clothes.

This set arrives rigged and prepared for Maya, so the deformation is already solved in the application the animation will happen in. That preparation is the difference between usable on day one and usable in a fortnight.

Six other builds sit on this page, from $139 for a static collection to $289 for rigged sets prepared for Cinema 4D and Maya. This set at $289 is aimed at emergency services visualisation, safety training material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2021.

Mobile Bay was one of the first Ticonderoga cruisers commissioned with vertical launch cells rather than the twin-arm rail launchers of the earliest ships. That change is the visible dividing line within the class: flat launcher decks fore and aft instead of rotating rails, alongside the four fixed radar panels on the superstructure.
The model carries the hull, superstructure, radar faces, gun mounts, boats and deck fittings, so the ship reads correctly from the waterline and not only as a distant profile.

At $289 it suits naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, museum and veterans material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2016, kept to real-world scale for correct placement beside other vessels.

Port Royal was the last Ticonderoga cruiser built, and being last shows: she carried the most developed configuration of the class, with vertical launch cells fore and aft, the four fixed radar faces on the superstructure and the helicopter hangar arrangement aft that the earlier ships lacked.
The model builds the hull, superstructure, radar panels, gun mounts and deck fittings, so the ship holds up at deck level as well as in silhouette.

At $289 it suits naval and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, museum and commemorative material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2016, kept to real-world scale so it sits correctly in a formation.
